fateExplorer.title: Fate Explorer
fateExplorer.description: Explore PFAS degradation pathways from the peer-reviewed literature. Built on 732 pathways extracted from 353 papers with DOI-traceable evidence.
whatItDoes: Maps parent-to-product degradation pathways for PFAS compounds
Shows observation counts, evidence scores, and temperature ranges from the literature
Identifies hazard levels and regulatory status of degradation products
Links every pathway to its source DOI for independent verification
howToUse: Select or search for a parent compound from the dropdown
Review the degradation products table — sorted by evidence score
Click any row to see the full evidence chain with verbatim quotes
Use the temperature and atmosphere filters to narrow results
useCases: Screen a fluoropolymer for known thermal degradation products
Identify whether a compound degrades to regulated PFAS (e.g. PFOA, PFOS)
Gather DOI citations for a regulatory submission or expert report
tips: Higher evidence scores indicate more independent observations across papers
Temperature ranges show the experimental conditions where degradation was observed
Products flagged as 'regulated' appear in EPA, EU, or Stockholm Convention lists

litigation.title: SENTINEL — Litigation Risk
litigation.description: Publication dynamics analysis and litigation risk forecasting. Tracks scientific attention trajectories using physics-inspired metrics (velocity, acceleration, jerk) derived from PubMed publication data.
whatItDoes: Tracks publication volume, velocity, acceleration, and jerk for PFAS compounds
Provides a GenX case study backtest against 412 PubMed publications and 14 key events
Forecasts litigation risk windows based on publication dynamics patterns
Maps the relationship between scientific attention and regulatory/legal action
howToUse: Use the GenX Case Study tab to see the validated backtest against real events
Switch to the Risk Forecast tab to view forward-looking projections
Review the publication dynamics chart — rising acceleration signals emerging risk
Check the timeline of key events to see how science preceded litigation
useCases: Assess whether a compound is on a litigation trajectory similar to GenX or PFOA
Identify the publication velocity inflection points that preceded past lawsuits
Support early-warning monitoring for compounds in your portfolio
tips: Publication count is 'position' — velocity is papers/year, acceleration is how fast velocity changes
Jerk (third derivative) spikes often precede regulatory action by 12–18 months
The GenX backtest is validated against real Chemours litigation timeline with 412 PubMed papers

tier1.description: Structure-aware compound screening combining Tier 1 (Morgan fingerprint similarity against 10,974 EPA PFAS compounds) with Tier 2 (substructure pattern mining with Wilson score confidence intervals from 732 literature pathways). Not a prediction engine — reports what the published literature shows.
whatItDoes: Tier 1: Computes Tanimoto similarity against the full EPA PFAS database and aggregates degradation endpoints
Tier 2: Detects substructure patterns (SMARTS + algorithmic chain analysis) and correlates them with endpoint buckets
Reports Wilson score confidence intervals — honest uncertainty, not fake precision
Tracks precursor resolution coverage so you know how grounded the correlations are
Returns DOI-cited evidence for every pathway found
howToUse: Enter a SMILES string directly, or use a quick-select badge (GenX, PFOA, PFOS, 6:2 FTOH)

useCases: Screen a novel compound by finding what happens to structurally similar PFAS
Identify substructure patterns (e.g., long perfluoro chain + carboxylic acid) that correlate with specific endpoints
Assess how well-grounded the correlations are via the coverage report
Gather literature evidence for compounds without direct study data
tips: The risk signal reflects endpoint classes: long-chain acids and sulfonates = HIGH
Tier 2 pattern badges are color-coded: blue = SMARTS, green = algorithmic, purple = classification
Confidence intervals show the plausible range — wide intervals mean few supporting precursors
The coverage report shows resolution rate — low coverage means rules are based on fewer compounds

product.explanation: A chemical compound formed when the parent material breaks down. Products can be intermediates (temporary) or endpoints (final).

productIntermediate.explanation: A temporary compound formed during degradation. Named P1, P2, etc. in order of detection. These often break down further into other products.

massToCharge.explanation: A measurement from mass spectrometry used to identify chemicals. Each compound has a unique M/Z value, like a molecular fingerprint.

confidence.explanation: How strongly the scientific literature supports this pathway. Based on the number of independent papers documenting this transformation. Higher percentage = more publications. This is not a statistical confidence interval.

mechanism.explanation: The chemical process by which the compound breaks down. Examples: thermal (heat), oxidative (oxygen reaction), hydrolytic (water reaction).

hazard.explanation: Potential health or environmental risk. Based on toxicity data and regulatory assessments. CRITICAL and HIGH warrant immediate attention.

regulated.explanation: Whether restricted by environmental agencies (EPA, EU, Stockholm Convention). Regulated = legal limits exist for this substance.

degradationProducts.explanation: Chemicals formed when a material breaks down under heat, UV, or other conditions. Important because some are more harmful than the original.

sources.explanation: Number of peer-reviewed papers documenting this pathway. More sources = higher confidence the pathway is real.

temperature.explanation: Temperatures at which degradation was observed in laboratory studies. Shown in degrees Celsius.
